caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 223 of 1996.
lawyer:
MA Wahhab Miah, Advocate, instructed by Shamsul Haque Siddique, Advocate-on-Record —For the Petitioner.  
Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record — For the Respondents.
parties:
Solaiman Mia (Md) ----- Petitioner
Vs.
People's Republic of Bangladesh & others  ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Bimalendu Bikash Roy Chowdhury J : This petition for leave to appeal by the plaintiff-petitioner is from the Judgment and order dated January 30, 1996 passed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3470 of 1994 discharging the Rule and thereby affirming those dated October 20, 1994 passed by the learned  Additional District Judge, First Court, Chittagong in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 236 of 1992 arising out of an application under Order 39, rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure in Other Suit No. 76 of 1991 pending in the Third Court of Assistant Judge, Chittagong. 

 2. The plaintiff-petitioner brought the said suit seeking a declaration that cancellation of his lease in respect of the house in suit was illegal and void. Briefly put, his case is that defendant-respondent No. 5 Md. Nurul Islam had lease-hold right from the Government in the disputed house. But one Harun-or-Rashid occupied the same from whom the plaintiff-petitioner had taken lease of the house. Subsequently upon an application to the Government the latter settled the house in his favour realising Taka 60,000.00 as penal rate. On or about August 29, 1991 the Government cancelled his lease disclosing the original lessee Nurul Islam had appeared to claim the property on his lease-hold right and that the plaintiff-petitioner's lease was obtained upon fraudulent suppression of facts. 

 3. Being apprehensive that he might be dispossessed from the disputed house before the disposal of the suit the plaintiff-petitioner filed an application for an order of temporary injunction restraining that the defendant-respondents from dispossessing him from the house in question. The prayer was opposed by defendant-respondent No.1 and 5 on the plea that the plaintiff-petitioner took the house on rent from the original lessee Nurul Islam under an agreement dated July 1, 1989 and later obtained lease of the house from the Government. 

 4. The learned Assistant Judge concerned initially directed the parties to maintain status quo in respect of the disputed house, but upon subsequent hearing vacated the said order on August 18, 1992 on the grounds that the plaintiff-petitioner had no arguable case and that the balance of convenience and inconvenience was against the plaintiff-petitioner. 

 5. The plaintiff-petitioner took an appeal therefrom. The learned Additional District Judge, First Court, Chittagong who heard the appeal maintained the order of the learned trial Judge refusing injunction. In revision, the High Court Division did not interfere with the orders of the Court below and discharged the Rule giving rise to this petition for leave to appeal. 

 6. Mr. MA Wahhab Miah, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-petitioner, has urged before us that the plaintiff ought to have been granted injunction in view of his prima facie case and the balance of convenience and inconvenience particularly when he is in possession of the disputed house. 

 7. It transpires that on consideration of the materials adduced by the parties, both the trial Court and the appellate Court concurrently found that the plaintiff-petitioner had failed to make out a prima facie case for injunction and that the balance of convenience and inconvenience was also against him. The learned Advocate for the petitioner could not show us that the findings of the courts below are either arbitrary or fanciful. In the circumstances the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division, in refusing to interfere with the appellate order in the exercise of his discretionary power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, committed no illegality. Again, it is worth noting that after vacation of the order of status quo on August 18, 1992 the plaintiff-petitioner does not appear to have been favoured with any order of injunction till today. When he could do without any order of injunction so long he seems not to genuinely need injunction at this hour. We thus find no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner.
